blocks.text: This is a seed. It is small and brown. We put the seed in the soil. We give it water. The seed waits in the dark. Then a root grows down. The root drinks the water. blocks.prompt: The Seed That Packs Its Own Lunch
blocks.text: Every seed has a tiny plant curled up inside it. It has a packed lunch too. The seed keeps a little store of food, right there under its coat. When the seed gets water, it swells up and the coat splits open. The root comes out first. It always grows down. Then the shoot pushes up through the soil. All of this happens in the dark. The little plant is eating its packed lunch. When the first leaves reach the light, the lunch is gone. Now the leaves can make food out of sunshine. The plant will feed itself for the rest of its life.

blocks.prompt: The Lunch Box Under the Ground
blocks.text: A seed looks like a small dead pebble. It is not dead. It is waiting. Crack one open and you will find a tiny plant already built inside, with the beginnings of a root and a leaf. Packed around it is a store of food. The seed is carrying its own lunch. The seed waits until three things arrive: water, air, and warmth. Then it soaks up water until its coat splits. The root pushes out first and turns down. The shoot pushes out next and turns up. Nothing down there can see. The seed does all of this in total darkness, running on the food it packed. That food does not last long. The little plant spends it climbing to the surface. If the shoot reaches the light in time, the leaves open and turn green, and the plant starts making its own food out of sunlight. If the food runs out first, the plant never comes up. Every seed is a small race.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: The Packed Lunch
blocks.text: Hold a bean in your hand. It is dry, hard, and completely still. It seems less alive than a stone. In fact it is a plant on pause, and it arrived packed with everything it needs to start. Split the bean along its seam. Inside are two thick halves and, tucked between them, a pale hook about the size of a comma. That hook is the embryo: a root at one end, a shoot at the other, a whole plant folded down to almost nothing. The two thick halves are called cotyledons, and they are the lunch. The parent plant filled them with starch so its baby would not have to find food on its first day. Germination begins with a drink. The seed soaks up water, swells, and splits its coat. The root comes out first and bends downward, no matter which way up the seed happens to be lying. Cells in the root tip hold heavy grains of starch that sink to the bottom, and the root simply follows them. The shoot does the opposite and climbs. None of this happens in the light. It is all underground, in the dark, powered entirely by the starch in the cotyledons. The seedling is spending an inheritance, and there is only a fixed amount of it. When the leaves finally break the surface and unfold, they turn green and begin building sugar out of sunlight, water, and air. From that moment the plant pays its own way. The cotyledons, emptied out, shrivel and drop off. The lunch is finished because it is no longer needed.

blocks.prompt: Where Does a Tree Come From?
blocks.text: Around 1640, a Flemish doctor named Jan Baptist van Helmont asked a question that sounds too simple to be interesting. A tree is heavy. Where does all that weight come from? Everyone already knew the answer. Soil. Plants sit in it with their roots buried, so obviously they eat it. Van Helmont decided to check anyway. He dried out two hundred pounds of soil, packed it into a pot, and planted a willow shoot weighing five pounds. For five years he added nothing but rainwater. Then he pulled the willow out and weighed it. One hundred and sixty-nine pounds. He dried the soil again and weighed that too. It had lost about two ounces. The tree had gained one hundred and sixty-four pounds. The soil had given up almost nothing. Van Helmont concluded that the tree was made of water, and he published that as fact. He was wrong, but he was wrong in the most useful way possible. His experiment did not find the right answer, but it destroyed the wrong one. Soil is not plant food. It took more than a century for others to track down the missing ingredient, and it had been hiding in plain sight the whole time. A plant builds most of its body out of thin air. Leaves take in carbon dioxide, an invisible gas that makes up about four hundredths of one percent of the atmosphere. Using energy captured from sunlight, a leaf strips the carbon out of that gas and locks it into sugar. The sugar becomes wood, root, leaf, and seed. The water van Helmont poured in mattered, but mostly as a raw material and as a delivery truck for minerals. The soil mattered too, though only for a trace of those minerals and for holding the tree upright. So the next time you stand under an oak, consider what you are actually looking at. Nearly all of that mass was drifting past as gas until a leaf pulled it down and made it solid. The tree is, in a real sense, built out of air and light.

6.title: The Seed That Packs Its Own Lunch
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Seed That Packs Its Own Lunch

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Endosperm is the food store in wheat, rice, and corn
Those three grasses supply close to half of human calories
A 2,000-year-old date palm seed sprouted in 2005
Domesticated wheat cannot scatter its own seed
The coco de mer seed can weigh 55 pounds
Orchid seeds pack almost no lunch at all

blocks.prompt: We Are Eating the Plant's Packed Lunch
blocks.text: Consider what happened at breakfast. If you ate toast, cereal, oatmeal, rice, a tortilla, or a bowl of noodles, you ate a seed. Not a product made from a seed. A seed, ground up. And you did not eat the part of it that was alive. You ate the food supply it had packed for its own baby. Every seed carries two things. The first is an embryo, a complete miniature plant with a root at one end and a shoot at the other, folded down to almost nothing. The second is a store of food to keep that embryo alive until it can feed itself. In a bean or a sunflower kernel, the store sits in two thick seed leaves called cotyledons. In wheat, rice, and corn, it sits in a separate tissue called the endosperm, a dense block of starch packed around the embryo like insulation. By weight, the embryo is a rounding error. The lunch is almost the whole seed. That lunch exists because a sprouting seed faces a problem it cannot solve by trying harder. It must reach sunlight before it can make sugar, and until it reaches sunlight it cannot make sugar. So it does not solve the problem. It funds it. The parent plant loads the seed with enough stored energy to pay for the entire underground journey, root down, shoot up, in complete darkness, on credit. When the first leaves break the surface and turn green, the loan is repaid, and the drained cotyledons wither and fall away. Human beings noticed the storage. Beginning roughly twelve thousand years ago, in several places independently, people started planting, selecting, and harvesting wild grasses whose seeds carried unusually fat endosperm and whose ripe heads did not shatter and scatter themselves across the ground. Those grasses became wheat, rice, and corn. Today those three species supply close to half of every calorie humans eat, and the overwhelming majority of that food is endosperm. Bread, rice, pasta, tortillas, porridge, and beer are, at bottom, packed lunches taken from somebody else. The arrangement is stranger than it first sounds, because it is not quite theft. A wild wheat plant that scatters its seed keeps its independence and its odds. A domesticated wheat plant cannot scatter at all. Its seeds stay locked to the stalk, waiting for a harvester, and the species survives only because we replant it every single year. In exchange for its lunches, wheat received something no wild grass has ever had: farmers, irrigation, weeding, fertilizer, and roughly five hundred and forty million acres of the planet's surface cleared and defended on its behalf. It is worth asking who is farming whom. None of this changes what a seed is. It is still a plant on pause, dry, patient, and holding its own supplies. Some hold them for a very long time. In 1963, archaeologists digging at the fortress of Masada in Israel found date palm seeds sitting in an ancient storeroom. In 2005, someone planted one. It germinated. Radiocarbon dating put the seed at roughly two thousand years old, which means it had been waiting in a jar, lunch packed, since the Roman Empire. It grew into a tree. It is still alive.
